title: What we know about MI6
summary: Josh and Chuck (with the transcript labeling Chuck as "iHeart Intro") explore MI6, the UK's Secret Intelligence Service. They cover its origins in the German spy scare and William Le Queux's yarns, the Secret Service Bureau, early chief Mansfield Smith-Cumming (C) and his invisible ink and foot story, World War One agents such as Cyril Bertram Mills, World War Two codebreaking at Bletchley Park and the absorption of the Special Operations Executive and its quartermaster Q-inspired gadgets, Cold War recruitment tactics and the Oleg Gordievsky defection (Operation Pimlico), the 1994 Intelligence Services Act and going public, the Vauxhall headquarters attacks and Skyfall, the Iraq War bad intelligence, modern recruitment and technology challenges, and a recent death of codebreaker Gareth Williams. The episode ends with listener mail about disaster movies, including Testament, Melancholia and Jurassic Park.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: The hosts open with light banter about pronouncing MI6 and introduce the episode on the UK's Secret Intelligence Service.

segments.title: Introduction to MI6 and secrecy
segments.summary: The hosts note that MI6 is the oldest continuously operating foreign intelligence service and that its public information is sanitized, making research hard.

segments.title: Naming, CIA comparison and MI6 origins
segments.summary: MI6 is described as Britain's rough equivalent of the CIA, and the name Secret Intelligence Service dates from 1920, with the call sign 'six' from World War Two. Fleming, le Carré and Bond are mentioned.

segments.title: Record keeping and early origins
segments.summary: The hosts discuss MI6's historically poor record keeping, the official history written by Keith Jeffery up to 1949, and the German spy scare fuelled by William Le Queux, which led to the formation of MI5 and MI6.

segments.title: Secret Service Bureau and legal cover
segments.summary: The Secret Service Bureau, known as the Bureau, housed both services and provided autonomy and plausible deniability. MI6 has less bureaucratic hamstringing than the CIA and has legal cover in Britain.

segments.title: Chief Mansfield Smith-Cumming and early spycraft
segments.summary: First chief Sir Mansfield Smith-Cumming signed with a green C and was known for his lost foot legend, disguises and search for invisible ink, including a gross seaman-based ink.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Short ad break before the World War One discussion.

segments.title: World War One intelligence
segments.summary: Early sources in Germany, such as agent B, reported on German harbors and fleet sizes. The hosts describe MI6 becoming established after World War One, monitoring Russia and the Americans.

segments.title: Agents versus officers and Cyril Bertram Mills
segments.summary: The hosts define agents and officers in MI6 terms. Circus director Cyril Bertram Mills was an agent who flew over Germany and provided intelligence on the Luftwaffe, which influenced Churchill against appeasement.

segments.title: Interwar and World War Two period
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the slow start of MI6 in World War Two and its human intelligence networks in occupied Europe.

segments.title: Bletchley Park and Kathleen Pettigrew
segments.summary: Signals intelligence at Bletchley Park was strong. Kathleen Pettigrew oversaw communications and was seen as the inspiration for Miss Moneypenny.

segments.title: Special Operations Executive, Q and teamwork
segments.summary: MI6 absorbed the rival Special Operations Executive, including its research group that inspired Q, based on Charles Fraser Smith. The hosts contrast Bond's loner image with MI6's teamwork-based operations.

segments.title: Cold War structure and targets
segments.summary: During the Cold War, MI6 focused on the Soviet Union and partnered with the CIA in 1948. Officers included Moscow men and camel drivers.

segments.title: Recruitment methods and the dangle
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the KGB's MICE recruitment model (money, ideology, coercion, ego), bribery and blackmail, and the dangle operation that creates double agents.

segments.title: Oleg Penkovsky and Oleg Gordievsky
segments.summary: Penkovsky supplied Soviet documents during the Cuban missile crisis. Gordievsky, a KGB officer recruited via interest in Western culture, was exposed by Aldrich Ames and signaled for extraction with a Safeway bag in Moscow, under Operation Pimlico.

segments.title: Gordievsky extraction and impact
segments.summary: Gordievsky was smuggled out of the Soviet Union in a car trunk in Finland, with a diaper change to foil dogs. His insight led MI6 to advise Thatcher and Reagan to tone down anti-Soviet rhetoric.

segments.title: Intelligence Services Act 1994 and going public
segments.summary: MI6 became officially acknowledged through the Intelligence Services Act 1994, which included Section 7 immunity for agents acting abroad, and moved to a headquarters on the Thames. The IRA attacked the building in 2000, and Skyfall depicted it blowing up.

segments.title: Iraq War intelligence failure and modern MI6
segments.summary: Bad intelligence on weapons of mass destruction before the Iraq War is described as MI6's lowest moment. Modern MI6 faces technology challenges such as facial recognition and AI, and the hosts joke about one source's claims.

segments.title: Modern recruitment and Gareth Williams
segments.summary: MI6 now recruits through job listings and applications. The hosts discuss the death of codebreaker Gareth Williams, found in a locked holdall, and a former KGB claim of Russian recruitment.

segments.title: Listener mail on disaster movies
segments.summary: Listeners Maria and Kirk suggest the films Testament, Melancholia and Jurassic Park for the disaster movie episode. The hosts debate whether Jurassic Park counts as a disaster movie.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and the iHeartRadio production note.
